claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
Ti alters the electronic and lattice landscape of CoCrFeNiTi.
Chemistry-dependent electronic or magnetic interactions can govern the energetic preference for an fcc-to-hcp transformation.
CoCrFeNiTi deforms predominantly by planar dislocation glide.
Ti suppresses a strain-induced fcc-to-hcp or similar phase transformation in CoCrFeNiTi.
A strain-induced fcc-to-hcp transformation can increase strength without compromising plastic deformation.
Transformation interfaces provide additional obstacles to dislocation motion.
Suppressing transformation-induced strengthening permits easier dislocation motion and lowers work hardening, hardness, and strength.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi is an as-cast, homogeneous, single-phase fcc solid solution without secondary phases or precipitates.
Mechanical deformation should be compared against a similar Ti-free alloy known to undergo strain-induced transformation.
CoCrFeNi is an appropriate comparator in which transformation-induced hardening is expected.
At ambient temperature and quasi-static to moderate strain rates, deformation is predominantly dislocation-mediated and diffusion is not thermally activated.
The relevant structural mediator is the absence of strain-induced transformation interfaces together with planar slip rather than forest hardening or transformation-induced twinning.
Dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries can trigger an fcc-to-hcp transformation in a related CrCoNi alloy.
CoCrFeNiTi should exhibit steady flow, low work hardening, and minimal diffraction evidence of deformation-induced transformation.
CoCrFeNiTi should retain lower nanoindentation hardness than comparable transformation-strengthened alloys.
The hypothesis is limited to near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi at ambient temperature, moderate strain, limited diffusion, and conditions where grain-boundary and precipitate effects are not activated.
Observation of a significant strain-induced transformation, or forested non-planar dislocation structures correlated with increased hardness, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
